title: Systems of Two Linear Equations, Part 3: Traps and the Fast Way

beats.say: In this video, we look at five mistakes students make with systems of equations, and then use Desmos to solve a system and to find an unknown constant with a slider.
Each trap is shown as a wrong line first, then the right line, with the reason it's so tempting.
Trap one. Suppose the solution is x equals five and y equals two, and the question asks for x plus y. Students stop after finding one variable, or report the wrong one.
Finish the job. The question asks for x plus y, which is five plus two. So the answer is seven.
Trap two. When you subtract one equation from another, you subtract every term, including the signs. Students often forget to flip the sign of the second term in the parentheses.
beats.wrong_why: The sign on −y did not flip

beats.say: Subtracting negative y is the same as adding y. So y plus y is two y. The x terms cancel, and the result is two y.
Trap three. Two lines with the same slope don't always give infinitely many solutions. Students see matching slopes and stop checking the constants.
Matching slopes with different constants give parallel lines, which means no solution. Infinitely many solutions need the constants to match too.

Trap four. In a ticket problem, the count equation uses one as each coefficient and equals the number of tickets. The money equation uses the prices and equals the dollars. Students sometimes swap the two totals.
The count of tickets, one hundred fifty, goes with the equation of ones. The total money, fourteen hundred, goes with the equation of prices.
beats.right_why: Counts with counts, money with money

beats.say: Trap five. To make the c terms match, we multiply the first equation by seven. Students multiply only one side of the equation, which changes the equation and breaks the balance.
beats.wrong_why: Only the left side was scaled

beats.say: Multiply both sides by seven. The right side becomes seven times one hundred fifty, which is one thousand fifty.
Desmos is often fastest for systems, especially with decimals. You type both equations exactly as given, and click the crossing point.

card.text: Type both equations, click the crossing

beats.say: Our example has decimals. Zero point five x plus zero point two five y equals four, and x minus y equals negative one. By hand, the decimals would slow us down.
Open a fresh graph. We'll type both equations exactly as they're written.
Type zero point five x plus zero point two five y equals four. Desmos draws the line without any rearranging.
Now type x minus y equals negative one. A second line appears.
Click where the lines cross, and then click the grey dot. Desmos shows five comma six, so x is five and y is six.

Check in the first equation. Zero point five times five is two point five, and a quarter of six is one point five. Together that's four. If the question asked for x plus y, the answer would be eleven.
Desmos can also find constants. In the system six x minus nine y equals fifteen, and four x plus k y equals ten, we want the value of k that makes the lines the same line.

card.sub: Find k for infinitely many solutions

beats.say: We graph both lines, and use a slider for k, then drag until one line lies exactly on top of the other.
Type six x minus nine y equals fifteen. Desmos draws the first line.
Type four x plus k y equals ten. Desmos notices the new letter k and creates a slider for it.
Drag the slider for k from zero down to negative ten. The second line rotates, and when k reaches negative six, it lands exactly on top of the first line.
The two lines coincide at k equals negative six, which matches what we found by algebra. Overlapping lines mean infinitely many solutions.
Now a practice problem. Solve x plus y equals ten, and three x minus y equals six. Pause the video, try it, and then watch the solution.
The y terms are y and negative y, which are opposites, so we add the equations. Every term is added, including the constants.
On the left, y plus negative y is zero, and x plus three x is four x. On the right, ten plus six is sixteen.
Divide both sides by four. Sixteen divided by four is four. So x equals four.
Substitute x equals four into the first equation. That gives four plus y equals ten.
Subtract four from both sides. Ten minus four is six. So y equals six, and the solution is four comma six.
Check in the second equation. Three times four is twelve, and twelve minus six is six, which matches the right side.
To recap. Answer the quantity the question asks for, and subtract every term of an equation, with the signs.
beats.item: Answer what is asked, subtract every term

beats.say: Matching slopes with different constants mean no solution. Scale both sides of an equation, and match totals to the right equations.
beats.item: Scale both sides, match the totals

beats.say: Use Desmos to solve a system quickly, or a slider to find a constant. In the next topic, we study linear inequalities.
beats.item: Desmos solves systems and finds constants
